doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: Why jazz parties and traditional jazz are mostly white
summary: She discusses the gap between traditional and bebop audiences, dancing versus listening, and the New York Hot Jazz Camp.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Wow. We had, last night at dinner we were talking a little bit about the jazz party scene. And I had observed over thee years that there were very few black musicians that seemed to be playing those things. And of course the audience was almost always all white.
Do you have an observation about why that is?

Well the only — I’ve done one. I did one jazz party. There’s a big — I don’t know what the word is, but there’s a big gap between traditional jazz and modern jazz. And most people in the traditional scene are white from what I can gather. And so, and then the modern jazz scene, or I won’t even say that, the bebop scene forward is a lot more mixed culturally. And I wonder why that is. I wonder why, because I certainly love swing and blues and Louis Armstrong and knowing where Bird and Diz came from and learning all that stuff. But you know I think it’s cultural really more so, you know, people, you know, I think that we, you know black folks probably want to feel like the way bebop came along, that we want to be listened to, not danced to, because I did my first swing dance, and this was not a jazz party but I love doing swing dances as well. And I did my first swing dance with Earl May with the great bass player Earl May. And Eddie Locke was on drums. And Eddie hated playing for dancers.

Hated it. So I think it’s a thing. I think it’s just a thing of I want to stretch out and solo and I don’t care if you dance. I want you to listen. So it may be that. It may just be that. And you know they don’t really teach tunes in school. That’s not a thing in a lot of schools. People don’t know tunes too much.
I don’t know what they think they’re going to do. They’re going to go out and play modes?

Yeah. They’re going to play original music, you know, and kind of mood music and stuff like that, and they get to solo, you know, long solos. So that’s kind of what I experience. And you know when I mention it to them, like “I’m in the Mood for Love” to some people they think it’s corny. They just think of Little Rascals or whatever.
It was Sylvester? No. The guy with the top.

With the, yeah. And so it’s interesting. It’s very interesting because I also have taught at the New York Hot Jazz Camp, which is going into its fourth year next year I believe. And I’m, besides Vincent Gardner, who plays with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, Wycliffe Gordon came and spoke, you know, at one of them. But Vincent taught. And we were the only two black people involved, and I think I’m right about that.

Yeah. There were two Asian students, and there were a few singers of color. I had a few black student singers. But other than that I looked around last year, this year, and I thought yeah, hmm, and then Evan Christopher was involved too so I’m wrong about that. But there are a very smattering of us, just a smattering.
